sentences.text: Xiongguanlong is a basal tyrannosauroid that is more derived than Eotyrannus, positioning it closer to the Tyrannosauridae family.
The skull of Xiongguanlong is very elongated compared to other tyrannosauroids, particularly in the maxillary, lacrimal, and postorbital bones.
Fused parietal bones feature a short, concave sagittal crest that served as an attachment point for bite muscles.
Analysis of dental alveoli revealed that Xiongguanlong possessed four premaxillary teeth and fifteen maxillary teeth.
The neck vertebrae have centra that are strongly fused to the neural arches and are concave anteriorly and convex posteriorly.
The cervical vertebrae possess pneumatic foramina, a feature not found in Albertosaurus, Daspletosaurus, or Tyrannosaurus.
Xiongguanlong was a bipedal animal that balanced its body with a long tail, like most other theropods.
The vertebrae were more robust than in other basal tyrannosauroids, possibly to better support a large skull with a long snout similar to that of Alioramus.
Researchers estimated the length of Xiongguanlong to be approximately 5 meters.
Based on regression analysis, the estimated mass of Xiongguanlong is approximately 270 kilograms.
The genus Xiongguanlong was described by Li and colleagues in 2009.
The generic name Xiongguanlong combines the former name of Jiayuguan City, "Xiong Guan," meaning "grand pass," and the Mandarin word "long," meaning "dragon."
The species name baimoensis refers to the "White Ghost Castle," a geological feature at the fossil site.
The fossils were found in the Xiagou Formation in the Yujingzi Basin of Gansu, China.
Mark Norell, Peter Makovicky, and a team from Beijing University discovered and prepared the fossils between 2006 and 2007.
The type species X. baimoensis was described online in 2009 by a team of researchers from China and the United States and formally published in January 2009.
The fossils include a skull, vertebrae, a right ilium, and a right femur.
Xiongguanlong was the largest known predator found in the Xiagou Formation.
Xiongguanlong was almost certainly an obligate carnivore, consistent with other known tyrannosauroids.
Unlike derived tyrannosaurids, Xiongguanlong lacked adaptations for generating strong bite forces.

Xiongguanlong was classified as a tyrannosauroid based on features including a vertical ridge on the ilium, a notch on the ilium's dorsal edge, fused nasal bones, and smaller premaxillary teeth compared to maxillary teeth.
In the phylogenetic analysis proposed by the authors, Xiongguanlong appears as a sister taxon to Tyrannosauridae and Appalachiosaurus.
It has been found that Xiongguanlong is closely related to Alectrosaurus.
Xiongguanlong lived during the Early Cretaceous period, between 124 and 113 million years ago.
Xiongguanlong is considered a middle Cretaceous taxon that helps fill a gap in the fossil record of tyrannosauroids during that period.
Evidence suggests some tyrannosauroids migrated to North America before 108 million years ago, a timeframe relevant to the era of Xiongguanlong.
The region where Xiongguanlong fossils were found was part of the Gobi Desert today but was likely near the coast of the Tethys Sea during the Early Cretaceous.
Xiongguanlong lived during the mid-Cretaceous period, approximately between 123 and 113 million years ago, from the Aptian to the Albian stages, in what is now Asia.
The time range for Xiongguanlong is the Aptian stage, from 121.4 to 113.2 million years ago.
Some authors debate whether the fossil record is sufficient to draw concrete conclusions about tyrannosauroid evolution and dispersal during the relevant Cretaceous period.

Body mass estimates for the mature Xiongguanlong specimen fall between those of late Cretaceous tyrannosaurs and Barremian tyrannosaurs, suggesting the trend of increasing body size in North American Tyrannosauridae may extend earlier in the clade's history, though phylogenetic work is required to corroborate this.

The thin, crestless nasals of Xiongguanlong contradict the recent hypothesis of correlated progression in tyrannosaurid feeding mechanics and suggest more complex patterns of character evolution in the integration of feeding adaptations in tyrannosaurs.
